title: User Mode and Kernel Mode: The Trap Door
topic: User mode vs kernel mode — programs run directly on the CPU in user mode; a trap instruction is the only legal way to reach the kernel for privileged work, and a return-from-trap brings the CPU back

beats.narration: How can a program run fast on the real hardware, and yet be unable to do anything dangerous?

elements.content: Manimo bobs in centre-screen
fast on the metal — but never trusted with the keys

beats.narration: The CPU has two modes. In user mode a program does arithmetic and calls its own functions — but it cannot touch the disk, the network, or other processes.

elements.content: User mode lane on top, with safe-ops list
Kernel mode lane on bottom, with privileged-ops list
Privilege boundary line between lanes
two modes, one CPU — and a wall between them

beats.narration: When the program needs something privileged, it executes a trap instruction. The CPU flips into kernel mode and jumps to a fixed handler chosen by the OS.

elements.content: x = read(fd, buf, n);
PC pulse marker on read() line
TRAP arrow drawn from read() line down through the boundary
Mode switches: user → kernel
Kernel-side trap handler entry point highlighted
the trap is the only legal door into the kernel

beats.narration: The kernel does the work, then a return-from-trap puts the CPU back in user mode, right where the program left off.

elements.content: 1. validate the args
2. read from disk
3. copy bytes to the user buffer
return-from-trap arrow drawn back up to the user code
Mode flips back: kernel → user
PC marker resumes on the line after read()
the program never noticed the detour

beats.narration: This is Limited Direct Execution. Programs run on real hardware — but the keys to the system stay with the kernel.

elements.content: Direct on the metal. Through the kernel for the keys.
(this is what we call Limited Direct Execution)
